subject: political-science
intro: Political science leads to paid work studying and shaping power — analysing political systems, reporting on them, planning the towns they govern, and teaching the next generation of voters and officials.

roles.title: Political Scientists
roles.what: Study the origin, development and operation of political systems — public opinion, political decision-making and ideology — and analyse the structure and operation of governments and political institutions.
roles.where: The democracy-and-participation, political-parties and electoral-systems units are the raw material of the job; the ideology units on liberalism, conservatism and socialism train the analysis of political thought the role performs.

roles.title: News Analysts, Reporters, and Journalists
roles.what: Narrate or write news stories, reviews and commentary for newspapers, magazines, radio, television and other media — collecting and analysing information about events, including the political ones.
roles.where: The voting-behaviour-and-the-media unit — election case studies and how the media influences politics — trains you to report politics critically, and the democracy unit's rights and pressure-group topics supply story frameworks.

roles.title: Urban and Regional Planners
roles.what: Develop comprehensive plans and programmes for how land and physical facilities are used across towns, cities, counties and metropolitan areas — balancing growth, environment and community needs.
roles.where: Democracy and participation — how citizens influence decisions through elections, referendums and pressure groups — is the political machinery planners navigate; the rights-in-context topic frames planning disputes.

roles.title: Political Science Teachers, Postsecondary
roles.what: Teach political science, international affairs and international relations courses at colleges and universities, combining lectures and seminars with their own research on political systems.
roles.where: The syllabus's parties, elections and ideologies units are the standard content of comparative-politics courses, and its democracy and suffrage debates feed first-year political theory teaching.
